## Best practice: name ports in detail before creating a REC

**Category:** Capella modeling best practice (component ports / REC-RPL)

**The practice:** Before turning a logical component into a Replicable Element Collection (REC), rename its function input/output ports from generic auto-generated labels (`FIP 1`, `FIP 2`, `FOP 1`, ...) to descriptive names that say what each port actually carries and in which direction.

**Why it matters:** A REC gets instantiated multiple times as RPLs. Once you have several replicas, you'll be looking at multiple ports that all say the same generic thing (`FIP 1`, `FOP 1`) on different components, with no way to tell them apart at a glance. Descriptive port names stay self-explanatory regardless of which replica or which side of a connection you're viewing — you don't have to trace back to the exchange or port list to remember what a given port is for. This matters most exactly when it's most tempting to skip: right before replication, when the naming is still cheap to fix and about to get multiplied across every copy.

**Concrete example from this project:** the master station's "Manage States" function and the "Control Machine" functions on its Operator/Line Control actors had these generic ports before renaming:

| Component | Port | Generic name | Descriptive name |
|---|---|---|---|
| Manage States | input | FIP 1 | Operator Commands In |
| Manage States | input | FIP 2 | Line Control In |
| Manage States | output | FOP 1 | Machine Status Out |
| Operator / Control Machine | output | FOP 1 | Operator Commands Out |
| Line Control / Control Machine | input | FIP 1 | Machine Status In |
| Line Control / Control Machine | output | FOP 1 | Line Control Out |

The naming pattern used: **`<what it carries> <In|Out>`** — the direction word makes the port's role unambiguous even out of context, and the "what it carries" half matches the functional exchange name it connects to, so tracing a wire from exchange to port to component is a straight name match rather than a lookup.

**When to apply:** any time a component is a REC candidate, or more generally any component whose ports will be viewed independently of the diagram they were created in (semantic browser, cross-references, another engineer opening just that component). Skip it only for components that will never be replicated and are always viewed with their full diagram context visible.

---

## Extension: the same practice applies to component exchanges and component ports

The practice above covered function ports (FIP/FOP) on a logical function. The identical reasoning applies one level up, to **component exchanges** and their **component ports** — Capella auto-generates these as `C 1`, `C 2`, `CP 1`, `CP 2`, etc., which is exactly as unhelpful once a component becomes a REC.

**Concrete example, same project:** two component exchanges were added connecting `Master TR88 Seven State` to its `Line Control` and `Operator` actors:

| Element | Generic name | Descriptive name |
|---|---|---|
| Component exchange: Line Control ↔ Master station | C 1 | Line Control Interface |
| Component exchange: Operator ↔ Master station | C 2 | Operator Interface |
| Master station's port to Line Control | CP 1 | Line Control I/F |
| Master station's port to Operator | CP 2 | Operator I/F |
| Line Control's port to the machine | CP 1 | Machine I/F |
| Operator's port to the machine | CP 1 | Machine I/F |

**Naming pattern used here:** for component-level elements (which are physical/logical links rather than directional function ports), name by **the counterpart the port/exchange connects to**, suffixed `I/F` for ports (`<counterpart> I/F`) and `Interface` for the exchange itself (`<counterpart> Interface`). Unlike function ports, component ports are bidirectional, so the `In`/`Out` suffix from the function-port pattern doesn't apply here — the counterpart's name is what disambiguates instead.

Note that a component exchange can carry more than one functional exchange's worth of data in both directions (here, `Line Control Interface` carries the `suspend`/`unsuspend` signals one way and the `abort`/`machine state complete` status the other way) — the component-level name describes the *relationship*, not a single data flow, which is exactly why naming by counterpart works better here than naming by payload.

---

## Refinement: not everything should be prefixed the same way after replication

When a REC's replicas are disconnected, elements that were shared become independent copies with identical names across machines (e.g. every replica has its own `Idle` state, its own `start` exchange item). Whether that's a problem — and what the fix should be — depends on **how the element is normally selected or viewed**, not on the element type alone:

- **Elements viewed inside a scoped diagram (e.g. States in a State Machine diagram)** — leave the names alone. A state machine diagram is already scoped to one component, so there's no ambiguity within it, and prefixing clutters every box while breaking any standard-vocabulary match the names were chosen to preserve (see the PackML/TR88 example elsewhere in this repo). If disambiguation is needed outside the diagram (Explorer tree, open tabs), rename the generic container object itself (e.g. `StateMachine 1` → `Filling Station State Machine`) rather than its contents.
- **Elements picked from a flat, unscoped list (e.g. ExchangeItems in an "allocate exchange item" dialog)** — qualify the name. There's no diagram context to rely on here; the name is the only thing distinguishing one machine's `start` from another's in the picker. A `<Component>.<event>` convention (e.g. `InfeedLoad.start`, `FillingStation.stop`) works well and doubles as a natural tag-naming convention if the items are ever exported to a real control system.

**The test to apply:** does the person selecting this element ever see it outside the context that already tells them which machine it belongs to? If yes (a flat picker, a global search, an exported list), qualify the name. If no (a diagram, a tree already expanded to the right branch), don't.
